newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Bank says mortgage-rate hike reflects market.
newsitem.headline: HK Bank says mortgage-rate hike reflects market.

text.p: HongkongBank said on Monday its decision to lift mortgage rates reflected a softer property market, and not a wish to cut its property exposure.

"We're a fairly conservative bank, so we thought it was appropriate to take that action," a bank spokesman said, referring to the bank's decision to raise its mortgage lending rate 0.25 percentage points to 9.25 percent.
Several banks have raised rates in recent weeks in response to expected lower volumes and prices in the residential sector.
"We're just responding to market conditions," said a HongkongBank spokesman, adding that the Hong Kong residential property market had "softened".
But he said the higher mortgage rate should not be seen as a move to prune its property exposure.
"We don't have plans to change our exposure to residential property. Residential property has been a good business. The default rate in international terms is negligible," he said.
Standard Chartered Bank told Hong Kong's TVB Pearl on Monday it was also increasing its minimum rate by 0.50 percentage points to 9.25 percentage points.
Standard Chartered said many banks were near the property exposure limits recommended by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) so had no need to offer low rates to attract customers.
Analysts said the market was cooling, as anti-speculative measures started to bite, and less property came on stream, hence the bank's decision to protect profit margins.

"I think the timing is very convenient -- it is all very well to increase your rate but you have to realise that August and September are also quiet periods," said Alan Hutcheson, banking analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Hutcheson said the first six months of 1997 had seen rapid home loan growth as banks fought for business.
ING Barings analyst Peter Redhead said Hongkong Bank's decision to raise rates was predictable, because volumes in the second half would be lower than the first half of 1997.

"The second half is going to be the half when they're trying to protect margins, but also build their deposit base in Hong Kong, because many of them have lent so aggressively in the first half," Redhead said.
Redhead said Dah Sing Bank Ltd had lent aggressively in the first half of 1997, then bundled up US$300 million of home loans and re-sold them in June.
The US$300 million deal meant it could reduce its property exposure by selling off the low-margin home loans, he said.
While selling the home loans, Dah Sing retained the customer long-term for higher-margin business like credit card lending, insurance and other banking products, Redhead said.
Analysts said some banks' property exposure had ballooned in the first half because of aggressive home lending.
"The Monetary Authority will be leaning on some banks to reduce their exposure," Hutcheson said.
